detail.longDescription: When you do git pull without any other arguments it first fetches all branches in the remote. With my project pulling from just the main branch I often end up getting output like this: (any potentially sensitive branch names have been edited, I don't actually have a bunch of branches called REDACTED) $ git pull remote: Enumerating objects: 131, done. remote: Counting objects: 100% (130/130), done. remote: Compressing objects: 100% (121/121), done. remote: Total 131 (delta 63), reused 7 (delta 7), pack-reused 1 (from 1) Receiving objects: 100% (131/131), 157.39 KiB | 2.54 MiB/s, done. Resolving deltas: 100% (63/63), completed with 7 local objects. From REDACTED 6d282363..841d6e8f REDACTED-skill -> origin/REDACTED-skill + cf89f065...5f4d7b09 corrections/REDACTED -> origin/corrections/REDACTED (forced update) * [new branch] REDACTED-tests -> origin/REDACTED-tests 6dc5ebfc..ec89f36a feature/agent-tests -> origin/feature/agent-tests bd47b322..48c2b47d fix/REDACTED -> origin/fix/REDACTED + a2f8e714...eeefe63e fix/hardcoded-path -> origin/fix/hardcoded-path (forced update) dc4f23e1..7d3d857e REDACTED_integration -> origin/REDACTED_integration 31999328..11f9a923 skill/REDACTED -> origin/skill/REDACTED Already up to date. I'd like to perform a focused pull that only updates the configured upstream branch, it should be able to run much faster for cases where the upstream branch is literally already up to date like in the above example. It is not possible using the @{u} notation unfortunately: $ git pull @{u} fatal: '@{u}' does not appear to be a git repository fatal: Could not read from remote repository. If you assume the remote is called origin and the upstream branch matches the current branch name this is fairly trivial but that is not always the case. It is totally possible for the remote to be called tadhg's-code/features and the upstream branch to be called a/the-"real"-code so git rev-parse --abbrev-ref @{upstream} which returns the remote name and branch name seperated by a slash can't be easily seperated to pass to git pull which expects them as separate arguments. The shortest simplest code I could come up with to properly handle any arbitrary remote and branch combo that only pulls from the upstream branch is this: CURR_BRANCH="$(git branch --show-current)"; UPSTREAM_REMOTE="$(git config --get "branch.${CURR_BRANCH}.remote")"; UPSTREAM_BRANCH="$(git config --get "branch.${CURR_BRANCH}.merge")"; if [ -n "${UPSTREAM_REMOTE}" ] && [ -n "${UPSTREAM_BRANCH}" ]; then git pull --ff-only --no-tags "${UPSTREAM_REMOTE}" "${UPSTREAM_BRANCH}" fi My goal is to set up this focused pull in a Makefile , but setting any part of this as a Makefile variable only lets it be inserted back as shell code which breaks with the quotes as I demonstrated so this whole thing has to be one single step in the make recipe which is way too long to expect a user to see and understand what the heck it is doing so I have to suppress the real rule from being printed as make is intended which I am not a fan of. considering how easy it is to do an unoptimized pull that also updates unrelated branches ( git pull ) and how easy it is to get the remote + branch reference seperated by a slash ( git rev-parse --abbrev-ref @{upstream} ) it seems crazy how complicated it is to specify the remote and branch to the git pull command. Am I missing something? Surely there is an easier way to do a "update the current branch downloading the minimum data needed" operation.
